8. Even More Integral Applications

8.3. Moments and Center of Mass

8.3 Learning Objectives

  • Understand systems of individual masses and laminae
  • Find the moment of a system about a given axis
  • Find the center of mass of a system of 𝑛 masses
  • Find the centroid of a system with one continuous mass

8.3.1. Motivation

Suppose we have 2 masses (of different mass) supported on a massless rod (picture 2 heavy weights held up by a thin wire in comparison. The wire has essentially no weight compared to the weights). Where could we put a fulcrum so that the system is balanced?

In Figure 1 Alexander Calder brings this concept to life through his art. He has created many pieces involving the balancing of weights held with wire as mobile sculptures, this one is called “Black and Yellow Dots in the Air”. He was originally trained as a mechanical engineer, and had some sculptors in the family.

In the physics sense, we need to balance the torque about a specific point.

In the 1 dimensional case, we need to balance the mass times the distance on both sides of our fulcrum. That is, if

𝑚1𝑑1=𝑚2𝑑2

the system will be balanced. From the sketch we see that 𝑑1=(𝑥−𝑥1) and 𝑑2=(𝑥2−𝑥), and doing a bit of algebra we can solve for 𝑥, the location to put the fulcrum.

𝑚1𝑑1=𝑚2𝑑2⇒𝑚1(𝑥−𝑥1)=𝑚2(𝑥2−𝑥)⇒𝑚1𝑥−𝑚1𝑥1=𝑚2𝑥2−𝑚2𝑥⇒𝑚1𝑥+𝑚2𝑥=𝑚2𝑥2+𝑚1𝑥1⇒𝑥(𝑚1+𝑚2)=𝑚2𝑥2+𝑚1𝑥1⇒𝑥=𝑚1𝑥1+𝑚2𝑥2𝑚1+𝑚2.

8.3.2. 1-Dimensional Moment and Center of Mass for Point Masses

Solution

The moment about the 𝑦-axis is

𝑀=∑𝑘=13𝑚𝑘𝑥𝑘=8(3)+4(−1)+7(6)=62.

The total mass is 𝑚=8+4+7=19. So the center of mass is at

𝑥=𝑀𝑚=6219.

8.3.3. 2-Dimensional Moment and Center of Mass for Point Masses

Now we move to looking at point masses on a plane (instead of on a line). Consider the moments about the 𝑥-axis and 𝑦-axis for objects in two dimensions (and also 𝑧-axis if in 3-D).

Let 𝑃1=(𝑥1,𝑦1), 𝑃2=(𝑥2,𝑦2), and 𝑃3=(𝑥3,𝑦3).

Then, how far is 𝑃1 away from the 𝑥-axis? It is 𝑦1 away from the 𝑥-axis! (Justify to yourself why the distance is the 𝑦 value and not the 𝑥 value of the point)

How far is 𝑃1 away from the 𝑦-axis? It is 𝑥1 away from the 𝑦-axis!

We can then think about the moment in the 𝑥 direction separate from the moment in the 𝑦 direction!

Warning

𝑀𝑥 is the moment about the 𝑥-axis, meaning we are asking how far the points are from the 𝑥-axis and use the 𝑦 values of the points for this! It gives the 𝑦 value of the center of mass point!

The opposite is true for 𝑀𝑦.

Solution

First

𝑀𝑥=∑𝑘=13𝑚𝑘𝑦𝑘=1(3)+3(−4)+4(1)=−5

and

𝑀𝑦=∑𝑘=13𝑚𝑘𝑥𝑘=1(2)+3(3)+4(−3)=−1.

The total mass is 𝑚=1+3+4=8. Then

𝑥=𝑀𝑦𝑚=−18𝑦=𝑀𝑥𝑚=−58

So, the center of mass is at (−18,−58).

8.3.4. Center of Mass of a Lamina

How do we find the centroid of a lamina?

Suppose we have a simple region ℛ︀ defined under the curve 𝑓(𝑥) between 𝑎 and 𝑏. Then using our usual method of taking finite sums to approximate what we want and taking the limit we cut the interval up into 𝑛 sub-intervals with width Δ𝑥 and height 𝑓(𝑥𝑖) where 𝑥𝑖 is the value between each sub-interval. Then the mass of each strip is

mass=density⋅area𝑚𝑖=𝜌𝐴(𝑥𝑖)𝑚𝑖=𝜌𝑓(𝑥𝑖)Δ𝑥

The moment about the 𝑥-axis (and remembering to think about how far away from the 𝑥-axis things are uses 𝑦 values, and how the strip is kind of like a point mass at the half of the height) is

𝑀𝑥≈∑𝑖=1𝑛𝑚𝑖𝑦𝑖=∑𝑖=1𝑛(𝜌𝑓(𝑥𝑖)Δ𝑥)(12𝑓(𝑥𝑖))=𝜌2∑𝑖=1𝑛(𝑓(𝑥𝑖))2Δ𝑥

And taking the limit as 𝑛 goes to infinity we have

𝑀𝑥=∫𝑎𝑏𝜌2(𝑓(𝑥))2d𝑥

Next, the moment about the 𝑦-axis is

𝑀𝑦≈∑𝑖=1𝑛𝑚𝑖𝑥𝑖=∑𝑖=1𝑛(𝜌𝑓(𝑥𝑖)Δ𝑥)(𝑥𝑖)=𝜌∑𝑖=1𝑛(𝑓(𝑥𝑖)𝑥𝑖Δ𝑥)

And taking the limit as 𝑛 goes to infinity we have

𝑀𝑦=∫𝑎𝑏𝜌𝑓(𝑥)𝑥d𝑥

Lastly, the total mass is what we get from adding up all the 𝑚𝑖 and taking the limit as 𝑛 goes to infinity so

𝑚=∫𝑎𝑏𝜌𝑓(𝑥)d𝑥

For a lamina made up of a region ℛ︀ under the curve 𝑓(𝑥) on [𝑎,𝑏] the centroid is the point

(𝑥,𝑦)=(∫𝑎𝑏𝜌𝑓(𝑥)𝑥d𝑥∫𝑎𝑏𝜌𝑓(𝑥)d𝑥, ∫𝑎𝑏𝜌2(𝑓(𝑥))2d𝑥∫𝑎𝑏𝜌𝑓(𝑥)d𝑥)

8.3 Section Summary:

  • We looked at the moments and center of mass of point masses in 1 and 2 dimensions.
  • We extended this idea to the centroid of a continuous mass called a lamina defined by the region under a curve.
